passage: When Masterji read out the marks under the banyan tree, Gurpreet had the highest in Class 6 of their village school near Moga: 47 out of 50. He wanted to jump on the bench and shout it. On the way to the handpump, he waved his paper at everyone. 'Forty-seven! Beat that!' Then he saw Shalini, who had scored 29, quietly folding her paper very small. Something in his chest pinched. Shalini was the one who had shown him how to fix his cycle chain last week; he'd never have managed it alone. Gurpreet folded his own paper and put it in his pocket. 'Shalini, the chain's slipping again,' he said. 'Can you look at it after school?' She brightened. 'Bring it to the tubewell.'

qa.q: Where did Masterji read out the marks?
qa.a: Under the banyan tree.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as he waved his paper?
qa.a: Proud and excited, wanting to show off his top mark.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet change the way he shared his joy?
qa.a: He put his paper away and turned to Shalini's strength, asking her to fix his cycle chain.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt when Gurpreet waved his paper?
qa.a: Embarrassed and small about her own mark, which is why she folded her paper so small.

grounding: A village boy who topped the class wants to show off, notices a classmate's hurt, and honours her different strength.

passage: In Mexico City, Señora Ruiz handed back the history tests, and Alejandro's had a gold star: the highest mark in the class. His whole body buzzed. At lunch he couldn't stop talking about it. 'I even got the bonus question. Nobody else did, right?' Tomas, beside him, kept eating his torta and said nothing. Alejandro stopped mid-sentence. Tomas had got a C. And Tomas was the one who drew the comics everyone passed round, the ones Alejandro could never copy. 'Sorry,' Alejandro said. 'I'm going on and on.' Tomas shrugged, but his mouth twitched. 'It's fine. You studied hard.' 'Want to make a comic about the Aztec emperor for the project? You draw, I'll write the facts.' Tomas grinned. 'Deal.'

qa.q: What did Alejandro's test have on it?
qa.a: A gold star.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling when he got the test back?
qa.a: Proud and excited; his whole body buzzed.

qa.q: What did Alejandro do once he noticed Tomas?
qa.a: He apologised for going on and on and suggested a project where Tomas's drawing and his own facts both mattered 👍

qa.q: How might Tomas feel during Alejandro's bragging?
qa.a: Quietly low about his C, so he kept eating and said nothing.

grounding: A boy in Mexico who topped the class catches himself showing off and remembers his friend's strengths.

passage:
'I'm just stupid,' Shankar said, throwing his maths paper on the bed. 'Fifty-two. Everyone else got seventies.'
Aparna Akka picked it up. 'Stupid? You got the whole geometry section right.'
'So? The total's still rubbish.'
'Look here.' She ran her finger down the page. 'You lost almost all your marks in one place. Word problems.'
He leaned over, sniffing. 'I always get confused about what they're asking.'
'That's one topic. Not your whole brain.'
'Feels like my whole brain.'
'I know.' She sat down beside him. 'What if we do three word problems every evening this week? I'll read them aloud with you first.'
Shankar wiped his nose on his sleeve. 'Only three?'
'Only three. If it doesn't help, you can complain all you like.' He laughed despite himself.

qa.q: Which section did Shankar get fully right?
qa.a: The whole geometry section.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when he threw the paper on the bed?
qa.a: Ashamed and defeated, calling himself stupid because others got higher marks.

qa.q: What wiser way of looking at the result did Aparna Akka show?
qa.a: Finding the one topic where the marks were lost, word problems, and practising three a day.

qa.q: How does Aparna Akka see Shankar's result?
qa.a: As trouble with one topic, not proof that he is stupid.

grounding: A boy who calls himself stupid over a low mark is helped by his sister to find the one topic to practise.

passage: When I got my English paper back in Class 6, I saw 38 out of 80 and wanted to crawl into a hole. I'm Farhan. I told myself I was the dumbest person in the whole school. I didn't go out for recess; I sat in the toilets reading the red marks over and over. My friend Ujjwal found me. 'You're not dumb. You beat me in science,' he said. That helped a little. Then I made myself actually look at the paper, not just the total. Most of the red was in one place: tenses. Past, present, all mixed up. That wasn't my whole brain. That was one thing. I asked Ma'am for extra worksheets on tenses. By the half-yearly, I had 61. Still not the top. But not a hole either.

qa.q: Where did Farhan spend recess?
qa.a: In the toilets, reading the red marks.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel on seeing 38 out of 80?
qa.a: Ashamed and crushed, wanting to crawl into a hole and calling Farhan the dumbest person in school.

qa.q: What wiser step did Farhan take after the first shock?
qa.a: Looking at where the marks were lost, tenses, and asking Ma'am for extra worksheets.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see Farhan?
qa.a: As clever, since Farhan beat Ujjwal in science, not dumb at all.

grounding: A child ashamed of a low mark learns to look at which topic went wrong and practise it, instead of judging the whole self.

passage:
Note by Mrs Pema Dolkar, Class 5 teacher, after the unit test.
Wasim scored 11 out of 25 in the maths test, and when I handed back the papers, I saw him push his quietly into his bag and put his head down. I know how hard he has been working; I have watched him stay back three evenings this month, redoing long division. At break I called him over. 'Wasim, your mark is low. But I can see how hard you're trying, and your division is much neater than in June.' He looked up as if nobody had ever said that before. His ears went pink. 'Really, Ma'am?' 'Really.' We agreed on two more evening sessions before the next test. He walked back to class standing straighter.

qa.q: How many evenings had Wasim stayed back this month?
qa.a: Three evenings.

qa.q: What did Wasim's pink ears and 'Really, Ma'am?' show?
qa.a: He felt seen and encouraged, surprised that someone had noticed his effort.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that steadied Wasim?
qa.a: She named his effort out loud, pointed out his neater division and planned more sessions with him.

qa.q: How does the teacher see Wasim's low mark?
qa.a: As one result, not the whole story; she values the hard work behind it.

grounding: A teacher's note records telling a boy with low marks that she sees his effort, and how it steadies him.

passage:
Wednesday
Diary, it's Pooja. Science results came today. I got 14 out of 30, even though I studied every night. I wanted to cry in front of everyone. But after class Dolma Ma'am stopped me at the door. She said, 'Pooja, I saw your notebook. You drew every diagram of the heart twice. That's real effort, and it shows. The marks will catch up.' I didn't know what to say. I just nodded, and my throat felt funny. Nobody had ever told me they saw me trying. At home I told Amma, and she made my favourite rasam. I still wish my marks were higher. But today didn't feel like the worst day any more. It felt like someone was on my side.

qa.q: What did Pooja draw twice?
qa.a: Every diagram of the heart.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when Dolma Ma'am spoke?
qa.a: Seen and moved; Pooja's throat felt funny because nobody had noticed the trying before 🥺

qa.q: What difference did Dolma Ma'am's words make on a bad day?
qa.a: Pooja felt someone was on Pooja's side, so the day no longer felt like the worst.

qa.q: How does Dolma Ma'am see Pooja's work?
qa.a: As real effort that will show in the marks later.

grounding: A child with low marks writes about a teacher who noticed the effort, and feeling seen on a bad day.

passage:
Thursday. Mridul caught Nikita at the gate. 'Tomorrow's Hindi test. Just tilt your paper a bit, okay? We're friends, after all.' Nikita laughed nervously and didn't answer.
Friday. In the test, Mridul coughed twice, the signal he had suggested. Nikita felt her face burn. She wanted to help him; they had been friends since nursery. But her hand stayed flat over her answers. She kept writing. Afterwards Mridul muttered, 'Some friend.'
Saturday. Nikita phoned him. 'I'm your friend. That's why I won't let you copy. If you get caught, it's both of us. Come over tomorrow; I'll go through the next chapter with you.' There was a long silence. Then, 'Okay. Bring the good pencils.'

qa.q: What did Mridul do in the test as a signal?
qa.a: He coughed twice.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling during the test?
qa.a: Torn and embarrassed, her face burning, pulled between loyalty to Mridul and staying honest.

qa.q: What did Nikita offer instead of her answers?
qa.a: To go through the next chapter with Mridul at her home on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Mridul see Nikita's refusal at first?
qa.a: As disloyal; he muttered 'Some friend.'

grounding: Over three days a girl pressured by a friend to show answers feels torn, says no, and offers to help him study.

passage: 'Jeevan, your friend wants to copy your test? Your Lokesh Mama knows that feeling. In Class 6, my best friend Raghu leaned over during a science test and whispered, "Show me number four. We're friends, na? Friends help." My stomach twisted two ways. I loved Raghu. He had stood up for me against the big boys all year. But if the teacher saw, we'd both be in trouble, and he'd never actually learn it. I covered my paper and shook my head. He didn't speak to me for two days. On the third day I went to his house with my notebook and said, "I'll teach you four, five and six before the next test." He grumbled. But he passed. And we're still friends, fifty years on.'

qa.q: Which question did Raghu ask to see?
qa.a: Number four.

qa.q: What was young Lokesh feeling when Raghu whispered?
qa.a: Torn, his stomach twisting two ways, between loyalty to Raghu and honesty.

qa.q: Which choice in the story kept both honesty and the friendship?
qa.a: Covering his paper, then going to Raghu's house to teach him before the next test.

qa.q: How might Raghu have felt during the two days of silence?
qa.a: Hurt and annoyed at being refused, and perhaps embarrassed too.

grounding: An uncle recalls a best friend using friendship to ask for answers, refusing, and offering to teach him instead.

passage: 'Parul, you want to know if I ever cheated? I nearly did, once. Your Pooja Bua was in Class 5, sitting in the exam hall with the fan clattering. I was stuck on the last sum. The girl next to me, Meena, had left her paper right at the edge of the desk, and the answer was there, circled. The invigilator was dozing in her chair. Nobody would ever know. Part of me wanted those five marks so badly. Another part pictured showing Amma my paper and knowing it wasn't really mine. I turned my face to the wall and tried the sum again. I got it wrong. I still remember that wrong answer, and I'm prouder of it than of any right one.'

qa.q: How many marks was the last sum worth?
qa.a: Five marks.

qa.q: What was young Pooja feeling when she saw Meena's answer?
qa.a: Tempted and torn; part of her badly wanted the marks, and part wanted to be proud of her own work.

qa.q: What choice in the story built young Pooja's strength?
qa.a: Turning her face to the wall and trying the sum herself, even though she got it wrong.

qa.q: How might Meena have felt if she had seen Pooja copying?
qa.a: Uneasy or let down that her work was taken without asking.

grounding: An aunt recalls being tempted by a classmate's answer when nobody was watching, and choosing honesty over marks.

passage: Five minutes left in the geography exam, and Sir had been called out to the office. The room went buzzy with whispers. Deepak was stuck on the map question: which river flows through Guwahati? Tenzin's paper lay open on the next desk, turned towards him. Deepak's heart thudded. Nobody was looking. He could glance, just once. Five marks. But then he'd walk home knowing, and Tenzin would never know what he'd taken. Deepak shut his eyes and pictured the map on the classroom wall, the big blue snake curling through Assam. He wrote Brahmaputra, not quite sure. When Sir came back, the bell rang. Walking out, Tenzin said, 'Brahmaputra, right?' Deepak grinned. He had got it himself, and his chest felt clean.

qa.q: Why had Sir left the room?
qa.a: He had been called out to the office.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he saw Tenzin's open paper?
qa.a: Tempted and nervous, his heart thudding, pulled between wanting five marks and wanting to be proud of himself.

qa.q: What did Deepak do instead of glancing?
qa.a: He shut his eyes, pictured the classroom map, and worked out the answer himself.

qa.q: What would change if Deepak had glanced at Tenzin's paper?
qa.a: He might have got the same answer, but he would have walked home guilty instead of with a clean chest.

grounding: With the teacher out of the room, a boy is tempted by a friend's open paper and chooses to work the answer out himself.

passage: Last Friday in the spelling test, Sunaina had copied three words from Pranav's paper when Ma'am turned to the board. She got 20 out of 20 and a gold star on the class chart. Everyone clapped. Since then, the star had glared at her from the wall every morning. She couldn't look at it. She couldn't look at Pranav either, and he kept asking what was wrong. On Wednesday, during library period, she went to Ma'am's desk, her mouth dry. 'Ma'am, in the spelling test I copied three words. I don't deserve the star.' Ma'am put down her pen. 'Thank you for telling me. That took courage.' She took the star down and gave Sunaina a list of those three words to learn. Sunaina felt lighter than she had all week.

qa.q: How many words did Sunaina copy?
qa.a: Three words.

qa.q: Why couldn't Sunaina look at the gold star?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, because she knew she hadn't earned it.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do with her unease?
qa.a: She admitted it to Ma'am, who took the star down and gave her the three words to learn.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling as Sunaina avoided him?
qa.a: Confused and a bit worried, since he kept asking what was wrong.

grounding: A girl who copied once and was not caught feels uneasy, and admits it to her teacher.

passage:
Monday. Preeti hadn't done the English homework, so she copied Urmila's answers on the bus, changing a few words. Ma'am gave her a tick and 'Good work!' Preeti felt a small thrill.
Tuesday. The thrill was gone. Something uneasy sat in her stomach like undercooked dal. When Urmila asked, 'Did Ma'am like yours?', Preeti mumbled and looked away.
Thursday. Preeti couldn't stand it. At lunch she told Urmila, 'I copied yours on Monday. I'm sorry. I won't do it again.' Urmila frowned. 'You could have just asked me to explain.' 'I know.' That evening Preeti did the next homework herself, slowly, crossing out and rewriting. It wasn't as neat. It felt better.

qa.q: Where did Preeti copy Urmila's answers?
qa.a: On the bus.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling by Tuesday?
qa.a: Uneasy and guilty, as if undercooked dal sat in her stomach.

qa.q: What did Preeti do on Thursday that eased the unease?
qa.a: Admitted it to Urmila, apologised, decided not to repeat it, and did the next homework herself.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel about Preeti's confession?
qa.a: A little hurt and puzzled, since Preeti could simply have asked for an explanation.

grounding: Over several days a girl who copied homework and got away with it feels uneasy, admits it and decides not to repeat it.

passage: 'Arnab, you were only worried Sir might have seen you look? Let your Rashmi Pishi tell you about my worst exam. Class 6, history. My eyes slid to Anjali's paper for one second, just to check a date. Then I spent the next hour sweating, sure Sister Mary had seen. My pen shook. I barely finished. She hadn't seen a thing. That night I felt relief. Then, lying in bed, a stranger question came: if nobody would ever know, would I do it again? I realised I'd only been scared of getting caught, not of being dishonest. Those are different, shona. In the next test, I kept my eyes on my own page, not because of Sister Mary, but because of me.'

qa.q: Which subject was the exam in?
qa.a: History.

qa.q: What was young Rashmi feeling during the rest of the exam?
qa.a: Frightened and anxious, sweating and shaking, sure Sister Mary had seen her glance.

qa.q: What question in the story changed Rashmi's thinking?
qa.a: Whether she would do it again if nobody would ever know, which showed her fear of being caught was not the same as caring about honesty.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel if she knew about the glance?
qa.a: Perhaps uneasy or let down that her paper was looked at without asking.

grounding: An aunt recalls fearing a teacher had seen her glance at another paper, and realising fear of being caught is not the same as honesty.

passage: The power went out halfway through the maths exam, and the hall went dim and stuffy. Ma'am walked the rows with a torch. In the gloom, Kamal's eyes drifted to Zainab's paper; he saw a number and looked away fast. His heart slammed. The torch beam swept closer. What if Ma'am saw? He hunched over, face hot, waiting to be called out. She walked right past. Kamal let out his breath. Then something bothered him. He wasn't upset that he'd looked, only that he might get caught. What would he do if the lights stayed off and nobody could ever see? He didn't like his answer. Kamal crossed out the number he'd copied and worked the sum again by the grey window light. It came out different.

qa.q: What did Ma'am walk the rows with?
qa.a: A torch.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as the torch beam swept closer?
qa.a: Scared of being caught; his heart slammed and his face went hot.

qa.q: What did Kamal do after asking himself what he would do if nobody could ever see?
qa.a: He crossed out the copied number and worked the sum again himself.

qa.q: What would change if Ma'am had seen Kamal glance?
qa.a: He might have been caught and punished, but he might never have asked himself the deeper question about honesty.

grounding: During a power cut in an exam a boy fears being caught after a glance, then asks what he would do if nobody ever knew.

passage:
'Rank one again this term, Yamini. Nothing less,' Papa said, not looking up from his newspaper.
Yamini's spoon stopped halfway to her mouth. 'Papa, what if I can't?'
'You can. Your cousin did.'
Later, in the kitchen, Yamini whispered to Usha Maasi, 'Some kids in my class have ways to see the answers. I thought maybe I could... just this once.'
Usha Maasi put down the knife. 'Because of Papa?'
'I can't breathe when he says rank one.'
'Then that's what you tell him. Not the cheating. The not breathing.'
'He'll be angry.'
'I'll sit with you.'
At dinner, Yamini's voice shook. 'Papa, when you say rank one, my chest feels squeezed. I'm scared enough to think about cheating. I'd rather get rank five honestly.'
Papa lowered his newspaper. For a long moment he said nothing. Then, 'I didn't know it was that heavy, beta.'

qa.q: What rank did Papa demand?
qa.a: Rank one.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when Papa said 'Nothing less'?
qa.a: Pressured and frightened; she felt she couldn't breathe and even thought about cheating.

qa.q: What did Usha Maasi advise, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To tell Papa honestly how heavy the pressure felt instead of cheating, since an honest lower rank is safer.

qa.q: How did Papa react when Yamini spoke?
qa.a: He was quiet, then admitted he hadn't known it was that heavy.

grounding: A girl under pressure to top the class tempted to cheat tells her father honestly how heavy it feels, with her aunt's support.

passage: In Class 6, my parents told me that if I didn't come first in the half-yearly exam, I'd have to leave dance class. I'm Afreen, and I remember that week as one long stomach ache. Jatin, from the next row, whispered that his cousin could get the answers in advance. For one whole night I thought about saying yes. Then I pictured Ammi finding out, and my stomach hurt even more. On Saturday I sat on the kitchen floor while Abbu was making tea and said, 'I'm so scared of not coming first that I nearly cheated.' He turned off the stove. He listened for a long time. That night he and Ammi said dance stays, whatever my rank. I came fourth. Honestly.

qa.q: What would Afreen have had to leave if not first?
qa.a: Dance class.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel that week?
qa.a: Anxious and pressured, as if the whole week were one long stomach ache.

qa.q: What did Afreen do instead of taking the answers?
qa.a: Told Abbu honestly about the fear and the near-cheating, and Abbu listened.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt when he turned off the stove?
qa.a: Shocked and concerned, realising how much pressure Afreen felt.

grounding: A child pressured by parents to top the class nearly cheats, then tells a parent honestly how heavy the pressure is.

passage:
Tuesday
Diary, it's Dhruv. Today in the science test I saw Rajni reading notes hidden inside her pencil box. I felt so much better than her. At lunch I told Kiran, then Mohan, then the whole table. 'Rajni's a cheater.' Everyone looked at her across the canteen. She stopped eating and went red. At first I felt clever. Then I watched her sit alone for the rest of lunch, and I felt sort of dirty. Cheating is wrong. But what I did didn't fix anything; it just made everyone stare. Papa says if something is wrong, tell the person who can fix it, quietly. Tomorrow I'll tell Ma'am, just her. And I'll stop saying it at lunch.

qa.q: Where was Rajni hiding her notes?
qa.a: Inside her pencil box.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel after telling the whole table?
qa.a: Clever and superior at first, then sort of dirty watching Rajni sit alone.

qa.q: What more mature step does Dhruv plan?
qa.a: Quietly telling Ma'am only, and stopping the gossip at lunch.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Rajni after Dhruv spread it?
qa.a: Humiliating and lonely; she went red, stopped eating and sat alone.

grounding: A child who scorned a cheating classmate by gossiping sees the harm and plans to tell the teacher quietly instead.

passage: At the village well near Dharwad, Lakshmi filled her pot and said loudly to the other girls, 'Vasudha copied from a chit in the maths test. I saw. Some of us study, and some of us cheat.' The girls gasped and whispered. Lakshmi lifted her chin, feeling tall. Then Vasudha came down the path with her own pot, saw the faces, and turned back without filling it. Lakshmi's grandmother, Ajji, had heard everything from the steps. That evening she said, 'You were right that cheating is wrong. But you used it to make yourself taller and her smaller. If it matters, tell the teacher, quietly, and nobody else.' Lakshmi's cheeks burned. The next morning she spoke to the teacher alone and said nothing more at the well.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi say Vasudha copied from?
qa.a: A chit in the maths test.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling as she lifted her chin?
qa.a: Superior and proud, pleased to look better than Vasudha.

qa.q: What did Ajji advise instead of gossip?
qa.a: To tell the teacher quietly and nobody else, rather than using it to make herself look taller.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt turning back without filling her pot?
qa.a: Humiliated and ashamed, seeing that everyone had been told.

grounding: A village girl who spreads news of a classmate's cheating learns from her grandmother to report quietly instead of gossiping.

passage:
Two weeks ago. Saurabh was stuck on his Hindi essay the night before it was due, and Tejas came over and helped him plan it, sentence by sentence. Saurabh was so grateful he said, 'I owe you big.'
Monday. Before the science test, Tejas whispered, 'Remember you owe me? Pass me your answer sheet when Sir turns round.' Saurabh's stomach dropped. He did owe Tejas. Didn't he?
Tuesday. Saurabh had kept his sheet covered in the test, and Tejas wouldn't look at him. At break Saurabh went over. 'I'm grateful, really. But I won't help you cheat. I'll help you revise for the retest, every evening this week. That's how I pay you back.' Tejas kicked at the gravel, hands in his pockets, then shrugged. 'Evenings at your place. Your mum makes better snacks.'

qa.q: What did Tejas help Saurabh with two weeks ago?
qa.a: Planning his Hindi essay.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when Tejas said 'Remember you owe me'?
qa.a: Torn and uneasy; his stomach dropped because he felt indebted but knew cheating was wrong.

qa.q: How did Saurabh repay Tejas honestly?
qa.a: He refused to pass his answer sheet but offered to help Tejas revise every evening for the retest.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel after Saurabh kept his sheet covered?
qa.a: Annoyed or hurt; he wouldn't look at Saurabh.

grounding: A boy who owes his friend a favour refuses to help him cheat and repays him with honest help instead.

passage: 'Siddharth, your friend says you owe him? Let your Amandeep Chacha tell you about Gurnam. When I was eleven, my bat broke before the inter-school match, and Gurnam lent me his, the best bat in the village. I scored my first fifty with it. I felt I owed him forever. Then, in the half-yearly exam, he pushed a chit towards me: "Write the answers for me. You owe me." My hands went cold. I did owe him. But not that. I shook my head and kept my eyes on my own paper. After school I carried his bat to his house and said, "Every Sunday, you and me, your weak subjects." He was angry for a week. Then he came on Sunday.'

qa.q: What did Gurnam lend young Amandeep?
qa.a: His bat, the best bat in the village.

qa.q: What was young Amandeep feeling when Gurnam pushed the chit?
qa.a: Torn and uneasy; his hands went cold because he felt he owed Gurnam but knew cheating was wrong.

qa.q: How did young Amandeep repay Gurnam in the story?
qa.a: By teaching him every Sunday instead of writing his answers.

qa.q: How did Gurnam feel about Amandeep's refusal?
qa.a: Angry for a week, then willing enough to come on Sunday.

grounding: An uncle recalls owing a friend a favour, refusing to help him cheat, and repaying him by teaching him.
